title: Repeat the List Back to Back
statement:
Given an integer array nums of length n, return a new array of length 2n that contains nums followed by nums again, in the same order.

In other words, position i and position i + n of the result both hold nums[i].

examples.why: The whole list, then the whole list again. Not [4, 4, 7, 7, 1, 1]: each element is not doubled in place.
One element gives two copies of it.
Duplicates inside the list are kept as they are.

hints: How long is the result, and where does nums[i] appear in it?
nums[i] goes to index i and to index i + n.
Allocate an array of length 2n once and fill both positions in one pass, or use a language-level concatenation.

explain.intuition:
The output is two copies of the input placed end to end, so every element has exactly two known destinations: i and i + n. One pass over the input fills both.

In everyday code you would write [...nums, ...nums] or nums.concat(nums). Writing the index version shows you know what that one-liner costs: one allocation of size 2n and a linear copy.
steps: Let n = nums.length and create out of length 2n.
For each i from 0 to n − 1, set out[i] = nums[i] and out[i + n] = nums[i].
pitfalls: Doubling each element in place ([4, 4, 7, 7, 1, 1]) instead of repeating the whole list.
Pushing onto nums while looping over it with a length that keeps growing: the loop never ends.

solutions.title: Fill both halves in one pass
solutions.idea: Each nums[i] is written to index i and to index i + n of a preallocated array.

solutions.title: Built-in concatenation
solutions.idea: The language already joins arrays: spread twice in TypeScript, list + list in Python.

followups: Return k back-to-back copies instead of two.
You only need to read the doubled list, never change it. How can you answer get(i) without building it at all?
